en: The Scripture Spoken by the Buddha on Protecting the Great Trichiliocosm, Volume One.
Transmitted by the Dharma Master and Tripitaka Śramaṇa [Amoghavajra] at the Temple of Indra’s Palace in the Kingdom of Uḍḍiyāna, North India.
Translated by the Imperial Subject Shi Hu by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard.
At one time, the World-Honored One was dwelling on the southern side of Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, within the Great Tree Forest of the Buddha’s domain.
He was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
among whom were the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, and the Venerable Gayākāśyapa.
The Venerable Nadī-Kāśyapa and the Venerable Mahā-Nadī-Kāśyapa;
the Venerable Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya and the Venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa.
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Bakula, the Venerable Vasubandhu,
the Venerable Kūṭila, the Venerable Vaśiṣṭha, and the Venerable Aśvajit.
The Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Subāhu,
the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Nandikeśvara,
the Venerable Revata, and the Venerable Cunda.
Thus, he was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī, made offerings to him,
honoring, respecting, revering, and praising him.
With robes, bedding, food, drink, medicine, rare curiosities, and precious objects,
he made offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus;
at that moment, the great earth suddenly shook.
A great cloud arose, covering everything, and a fierce wind blew;
thunder roared and crashed, lightning flashed and struck,
and a heavy rain of hail fell, pouring down everywhere.
Throughout the ten directions, the darkness was so profound that the constellations were obscured;
the sun and moon did not appear and could not shed their light.
The sun lacked its warmth and possessed no radiance.
The people were filled with fear.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure divine eye,
beheld the king, ministers, and citizens of the great city of Vaiśālī.
Such calamities as these arose in competition with one another.
Furthermore, there were the Licchavis and others from Vaiśālī, as well as the queens,
concubines, and court ladies within the inner palace.
They are tormented and harmed by ghosts and spirits;
so too are kings, princes, and all those old or young,
as well as servants, attendants, and their entire retinues.
They were all being tormented, harmed, deluded, and distracted by ghosts and spirits.
This included all the people of that great city of Vaiśālī,
as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
They were all terrified, fainting with panic and alarm;
their body hair stood on end as they looked upward,
wailing and crying out these words:
Namo buddhāya. Namo dharmāya. Namo saṃghāya.
With single-minded devotion, they take refuge and beg for protection.
There may also be brahmins and elders who do not believe in the Triple Gem and instead turn toward Brahmā and the kings.
Some take refuge in Śakra, the Lord of Devas;
some take refuge in the Four World-Protecting Kings;
and some take refuge in Maheśvara.
Or the yakṣa general Ratnabhadra, the yakṣa general Pūrṇabhadra, and the Mother Hārītī;
the sun, moon, stars, and constellations; mountains, forests, medicinal herbs, and trees;
rivers, streams, ponds, and lakes; gardens, groves, stupas, and temples.
Whosoever is attached to their respective pleasures shall all pay homage and reverence,
saying these words:
"May this calamity, fear, and distress of mine [be pacified]."
"Who can provide salvation? How may I quickly attain liberation?
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all sentient beings, manifested auspicious signs and performed miraculous transformations.
By virtue of these practices, the devas, humans, and asuras of this trichiliocosm hear his voice and,
giving rise to a mind of reverence, all assemble together.
At that time, Brahmā Sahāmpati, lord of the Saha world,
together with the host of Brahmā devas and their sons,
and Śakra, Lord of Devas, together with the host of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, [were present].
The Four Great Heavenly Kings were present together with the hosts of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
the twenty-eight great yakṣa generals were present together with thirty-two powerful yakṣas;
and Hārītī was present together with her sons and her retinue.
During the night, she came to the place where the Buddha was;
with her own majestic radiance,
the Mother Haritī shone so brilliantly that Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa was illuminated, becoming one uniform color.
They approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet,
and stood to one side; then, with one voice and in unison,
they praised the Tathāgata by reciting these verses:
With a majestic golden form like the pure full moon,
as wealthy as Vaiśravaṇa, a treasury of auspicious jewels,
walking like a lion, and possessing the majesty of a great nāga.
A towering mass of pure gold, with the hue of Jāmbūnada,
like the clear moon in the dark night dwelling amidst the host of stars,
you manifest a brilliant and majestic appearance before the assembly of śrāvakas.
Homage to the Bhagavat, the most honored among gods and humans,
who brings benefit to gods and men; who dwells in the world to bestow protection and guards the Great Trichiliocosm Sūtra,
as previously taught by the Buddhas of the past.
Extending to the very edge of this Cakravāḍa mountain range, I establish the Vajra-bondary.
I bow my head to the Honored One among Men; I take refuge in the Fearless One.
With palms joined in reverent salutation, I pay homage to the Great Dharma King, the Muni.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent for the duration of a single thought-moment,
then addressed the Four Great Kings, saying:
"Great Kings, you should now manifest these various appearances and distinct forms."
"How do you disturb and trouble my disciples?
Great King, if there is anyone who, upon hearing of the appearance in the world of the Buddha,
the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, gives rise to a heart of joy..."
Such persons as these, within the Buddha-dharma,
plant the seeds of bodhi and are born at a time when a Buddha has appeared in the world;
they encounter pratyekabuddhas, arhats, and the assembly of śrāvakas.
Having planted the roots of all virtues within the Buddha-dharma and being fully endowed with the ten wholesome paths of action,
after the end of their life, they shall attain rebirth in the Heaven of the Thirty-two Devas.
In each of these heavens, they shall become a celestial king and experience heavenly bliss.
He was reborn among humans as a wheel-turning king (cakravartin),
ruling over the four kings and the four continents under heaven;
even unto the great oceans, all were brought under his single domain.
He obtained the perfection of the seven treasures and was surrounded by a thousand sons.
Those thousand sons of the king were wise and discerning,
courageous and diligent, and free from all fear.
Possessing exquisite and upright features, they have great supernormal powers;
as swift as the wind and possessing sovereign majesty and virtue, they are able to subdue enemies.
By these causes and conditions, they obtain such fruits of merit and fortune.
Attached to sensual desires, you indulge yourselves in pleasure and self-indulgence.
Now, in the presence of the Tathāgata,
you give rise to a mind of arrogance and manifest such signs and perform such deeds.
When they give rise to contempt, fear, and malice toward my disciples,
at that time Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King and Lord of the Yakṣas of the Northern Quarter,
shall immediately rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, and [proceed].
Kneeling on his right knee with palms joined in reverence,
he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
in the place where I now reside, there is a great city as well as various villages."
Gardens with flowers and fruits, palaces and towers,
surrounded by railings and stairways of gold and silver,
were all adorned with various kinds of precious objects.
It was stabilized by a stupa-pole with bells suspended on all four sides;
a wondrous net of pearls covered it from above,
and various famous incenses were burned, their fragrance wafting through the air day and night.
Various flowers were scattered, covering the ground;
it was pure, bright, and exceedingly delightful.
Hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens surrounded it on all sides.
Abiding therein, I experienced the pleasures of the five desires without ever being satiated;
like a person intoxicated and deluded, I was unable to awaken,
committing transgressions against my conduct and violating my original vows.
For this reason, the hosts of yakṣas roam throughout the world in all ten directions,
running about to drink blood and devour flesh—
whether they be men or women, boys or girls.
Upon such persons as these, various possessing spirits,
as well as those who consume evil food— those who eat blood,
those who eat flesh, and those who eat fetuses— will descend.
Those who eat raw flesh,
those who consume life,
or those who take birth as animals and various other species.
Or I may become a lion that constantly preys upon sentient beings,
perpetually killing and devouring their lives.
Great Virtuous World-Honored One, I now, before the Buddha and the fourfold assembly, [confess].
It is said that the physical appearances manifested by those yakṣas consist of various forms and features, each distinct from the others;
all these hosts of yakṣas possess the power of possession and bewitchment.
Therefore, I constantly hold a precious stūpa within which a sacred image is enshrined.
Among the hosts of yakṣas who possess and bewitch others, I am known as the Great King;
these yakṣas burn various kinds of incense.
They shall light various lamps and scatter diverse flowers as offerings to the stūpas and images, and as offerings to me.
World-Honored One, if there are hosts of yakṣas who act as possessing spirits, [they shall likewise do so].
They cause those sentient beings to manifest such signs:
either constantly laughing and rejoicing, or constantly being terrified;
or constantly weeping and wailing, or speaking excessively without measure.
If one is constantly deranged, or does not sleep;
if the body is in constant pain, or one gazes upward at the void;
if one delights in observing the stars and constellations, or is constantly running about.
If one finds no pleasure by day but rejoices at night,
or if one constantly envies these yakṣas,
such are the signs of being possessed by them.
"There is no one in all the worlds who can restrain them;
yet I possess a divine mantra capable of subduing them all.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave to speak it."
Then he spoke the mantra, saying:
Oṃ arye araṇi jaṃbhe akhaṇḍe makhaṇḍe kha-khaṇḍe khāhā hī hī.
Hare hāre hiri hīre hulu hūle hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā | Svasti sarvatraidhātukavaiśvāsana-samaye svāhā ||
*Mahārājña-namā-mamale-niścarī-dhipataye svāhā.* At that time,
the Gandharva King Dhṛtarāṣṭra from the eastern direction [spoke].
Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha,
and having paid respectful homage, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, among those of us yakṣas who possess people through bewitchment,
such various physical appearances as these manifest:
they may constantly sing and dance, or they may be fond of adornments.”
Whether they are free from craving, or their speech is truthful and reliable;
whether they are suddenly angry or suddenly joyful, or again, feverishly parched with thirst;
whether their eyes are as red as cinnabar, or suffering from malaria.
If one acts as if poisoned, keeps the eyes closed without opening them, remains constantly in sleep,
or always looks away with the face not turned toward the entrance—
such persons are possessed by yakṣas.
There is no one in all the worlds who can restrain them;
yet by means of my divine mantra, I shall bring them all under control.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave to speak it.
He then spoke the mantra:

Oṃ ākhe makhe vinākhe mande vārande zapale vākhe vakhani ākheli vaheli bhavanale vaśi vamocariṣṭi svāhā. Mucilinda! Gandharva-graha-vijṛmbhita-raśmi-mahārāja-sannāma-vāri-naiḥśvarya-dhipate svāhā. At that time, the Lord of the Kuṇapa, the Northern Heavenly King Virūpākṣa...
Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha,
paid respectful homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Bhagavān, if those among my gaṇas of kumbhāṇḍas who have been possessed by spirits manifest various such forms and appearances—
whether speaking excessively or suffering from parching thirst.
If the mind is confused and the eyes are dull and staring; if the face is flushed red;
if one constantly lies on the ground; if the body is perpetually cramped and tense;
if the countenance is ugly and hideous; or if the body is emaciated and wasted.
If one has long fingernails or long hair;
if the body is foul-smelling or covered in dust and filth;
or if one constantly speaks falsehoods or one's speech is deranged.
Beings such as these are possessed by kūṭaṇṭhas;
there is no one in all the worlds capable of subduing them.
I possess a divine mantra that shall bring them all under control.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave to speak it.
Then he spoke the mantra, saying:
Oṃ kha kha khame khala me khala me khara le khara.
Khecarī Kāśinī Kāruṇikā Karuṇākarī Kāmavibodhinī Bhairaveśī Jayaśvati Samayasamaye Śāmyantu me sarvamantrāḥ svāhā.
HŪṂ SVĀHĀ SARVASATTVĀNĀM GṚHṆA HOṢAYA PARAVĪROCAYA MAHĀRĀJAŚĀN MĀVALI NAIḤ ŚVARĪTIDHĀPAḤ.
*Ṭye svāhā*. At that time, the Western Dragon Lord, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa,
rose from his seat and bared his right shoulder.
Placing his right knee on the ground and joining his palms toward the Buddha,
he paid respectful homage and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as for us nāgas and others who are possessed by malevolent spirits..."
They manifest various such forms and appearances:
some are constantly hiccoughing or gasping for breath with long sighs;
some have their bodies perpetually cold, while others spit out saliva and froth from their mouths.
If one is prone to excessive sleep; if the body is as smooth and hard as a snake;
if the mind is courageous and undaunted by birth and death; or if one can run about without ever experiencing fatigue.
If their fingernails are long and sharp, or if they claw the ground with their hands until it is like a hollow pit—
such persons as these are possessed by various nāgas and others,
and there is no one in all the world capable of subduing them.
"I possess a divine mantra that shall bring all under subjugation.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to recite it.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:
Oṃ kṛyāse kṛkaśe kṛkaśe kaśaye kuru keke kūṭe khaṃge kuru ru akhare samakhare kāhuṃge aru.
Kye ga lu kye i ri śvi ri i ri mi ri dhi ri gu ru ba ti svaḥ siddhye ṣṭu vīraṣṭakṣa mahārājña namo vaḥ.
*Laṇaiśvarīye dhipataye svāhā.* At that time,
the World-Honored One uttered this great lion’s roar amidst the assembly of all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other spirits, saying:
I am the Great Man who tames all the world, the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses,
I bring those who are difficult to subdue into a state of discipline and compliance.
I now turn the Great Wheel of Dharma.
Alone and by myself, I shall subdue you great yakṣa generals and cause your entire host of armies to be completely subdued.
Now, by means of my great power of wisdom,
desiring to protect, benefit, and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings,
the Tathāgata has attained accomplishment in all *siddhis*.
"I possess a divine mantra named Sarvavidyā. You should listen and receive it;
I shall now recite the mantra: Oṃ asanigāṅgavate malanirghoṣe."
Hūṃ śū śūra-vajra-saṃvara-dhāri-satva-nirghāta-śarīra-vijaye-vigati-vara-guṇa-prabhate.
Arani-dharma-ucite niḥśeṣa-kṛtsna-svastyayana-satvānām āhīṃ sarva-sattvānāṃ tathāgatamātṛ.
Oṃ namo śvaretipataye svāhā. At that time,
the great yakṣas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and others from the four directions—
Upon hearing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, proclaim this divine mantra,
they all simultaneously joined their palms; struck with fear, their complexions turned pale,
and their bodies and limbs trembled with dread and agitation.
Unable to suppress it, he let out a great cry of terror;
its sound resounded far and wide, heard and known throughout the ten directions.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings then reflected upon the majestic power of the Great Thousand-Vehicle Great Bright King Divine Mantra, which is protected by the Tathāgata’s three secrets.
It is vast, profound, and inconceivable.
Upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken, all those yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and various spirits were completely subdued.
Just as a great wind blows away a flame until nothing remains,
so too is the Dharma taught by the Buddha like a sharp blade that utterly severs all poisonous and harmful thoughts.
The Buddha said: "It is like the mantra of Brahmā;
it shall destroy that eldest son of Kubera and cause that eldest son not to give rise to any heterodox thoughts."
Furthermore, if there are those who are afflicted, harmed, deluded, or possessed by those gods,
nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and various spirits;
One should take clarified butter and mustard seeds,
empower them with this divine mantra,
and cast them into the fire to cause flames to burst forth.
Furthermore, they may cast [the image] in the four directions as well as above and below,
or cast it into water;
these people will swiftly attain peace and happiness.
If there are those who do not comply with this mantra,
one should burn ghee mixed with mustard seeds;
causing them all to emit flames, they shall likewise attain peace and happiness.
Those yakṣas were struck by clubs;
their bodies broke out in sores and bore the marks of the clubs.
Those yakṣas suffered from intense pain and affliction.
He went to the royal city of Aṇakāvatī;
having arrived, Kumbhīra, by means of his majestic power and supernatural might,
commanded the yakṣas not to allow him to enter.
They were unable to eat or drink, nor could they remain in their original seats;
amidst the assembly, which was filled with various fears,
a great sound resounded.
In this realm of the yakṣas, which protects this profound sūtra of the great trichiliocosm,
should there be any yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, or other spirits who do not comply with it, [may they be subdued].
Those yakṣas and spirits, becoming greatly enraged,
were struck on the head with a vajra by the Vajrapāṇi Vidyārāja,
who then severed their tongues with a sharp blade.
Furthermore, they may use sharp knives to cut off their ears and noses;
or they may hack and sever them until their bodies are crushed to pieces;
or they may use a wheel of blades to decapitate them.
Some are constantly lashed with iron clubs;
some have their hearts pinned with iron spikes;
and from the mouths of others, pus and blood constantly flow forth.
Those who slander this sutra shall receive such retribution:
they will dwell perpetually in saṃsāra, emerging only to enter it again without respite;
they shall never again encounter any auspicious lands, kingdoms, or cities.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings—
the Eastern Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Southern Virūḍhaka, the Western Virūpākṣa, and the Northern Vaiśravaṇa—
donned the armor of patience and each sat upon a noble seat within the assembly of the Buddha.
The Great Brahma King, by means of his supernormal powers,
manifested a jeweled palace adorned with various kinds of exquisite gems.
Within it appeared a vajra-jeweled throne, upon which the Buddha sat.
That Great Brahmā King and all the Brahmā kings joined their palms in prostration, stood before the Buddha,
and praised the World-Honored One, speaking these words:
Like a banner of pure gold, his golden complexion shone brilliantly;
his eyes were like lotus flowers, pure and stainless;
he was like a king of sāla trees with its flowers in full bloom.
Like the pure full moon surrounded by a multitude of stars,
with majestic marks and signs and adorned with sublime virtues,
the Muni, the Dharma King, is a lamp for the world.
Devas and humans praise it as that which can bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings,
enabling them all to reach the ultimate shore of *nirvāṇa*,
and giving birth to Buddhas, *pratyekabuddhas*, and the assembly of *śrāvakas*.
The devas, humans, ṛṣis, brahmins, and others all increased in prosperity.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahābrahmā, the assembly of Brahmās, the Four World-Protecting Kings, and the rest.
And he spoke these words: "The Tathāgata, desiring to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings, has taught this;
you should listen and receive it.
Furthermore, if there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sūtra, slights or reviles it..."
It is, for example, as if someone were to shake Mount Sumeru and the four great oceans,
even turning the entire earth upside down;
that person would further say [of the shaking] of the sun, moon, stars, water, fire, wind, and so forth.
That I could bind such persons and transport them to another place so that they would appear there—
this is impossible, for they would only be deceiving themselves. This remains true even for those who,
having conceived various contrary thoughts, treat them with contempt and derision.
Such people as these are all driven by jealousy;
they do not act for the benefit of all humans and devas,
but instead act out of a fondness for increasing the hosts of bhūta spirits and other such beings.
Those various ghosts and spirits roam everywhere,
watching for an opportunity to seize people and devour their flesh;
such persons as these immediately become part of the retinue of all the Māras.
With *bhūta* spirits as their retinue,
such persons as these do not give rise to faith or reverence toward this divine mantra;
yet, by the power of the majesty of this divine mantra—
To cause those people to recognize their transgressions and evils,
they shall, before the Buddha, with a sincere mind, receive and uphold this *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī-dhāraṇī-sūtra* and perform repentance.
These people immediately became free from various punishments.
Then the great assembly prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
each gazing up with reverence at his golden body.
At that time, there was also the devaputra Viśvakarman,
who fashioned for the Four Heavenly Kings four great precious chariots,
each of which was composed entirely of the seven treasures.
That is to say, it was adorned with various interspersed jewels, such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, agate, crystal, and coral.
The Four World-Protecting Kings sat upon their precious chariots;
through their celestial power, they were all transformed into a golden hue,
and traveling through the air, they arrived at the kingdom of Potala.
Incense, flowers, and precious objects completely covered the ground as an offering.
At that time, the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings commanded sixty great yakṣa generals, saying:
Now that you all hold this divine mantra,
go forth in the four directions by the power of the mantra to [subdue] all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and other spirits.
"You shall bind his neck with a lasso and bring him here. Furthermore,
wherever this most supreme and profound sutra exists, throughout all lands in the ten directions, you must provide protection for it in every such place."
At that time, the assembly of Brahmā and all the other devas,
by means of the power of this profound sūtra and its divine mantras,
subdued all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and other spirits.
And so he acts as the protector of the great trichiliocosm.
At that time, the Great Yakṣa Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Heavenly Kings,
immediately travels through the four directions to patrol the world.
He commanded all the great yakṣa generals:
"All you yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and spirits,
whether you dwell in the lands, cities, and towns of the ten directions, or reside in mountain caves."
In the east, the yakṣa-māra is accompanied by a host of twenty-eight bhūta spirits;
in the south, the kūṣmāṇḍa-māra is accompanied by a host of twenty-eight bhūta spirits.
In the west, the nāga-māyāvins were accompanied by a host of twenty-eight bhūta spirits;
in the north, the yakṣa-māyāvins were accompanied by a host of twenty-eight bhūta spirits.
Such various types of possessing spirits constantly afflict and harm sentient beings in the world, performing all manner of demonic acts.
You great yakṣa generals, [should restrain them].
By the power and majesty of this divine mantra, they were subdued;
with five nooses, their bodies were bound and they were dragged here.
When Kuvēra had spoken these words, [the assembly]...
Furthermore, there is the eldest son of Kūṭadanta named Sañjaya,
a great yakṣa who constantly rides upon humans and commands a host of sixty koṭis of yakṣas and bhūta spirits.
His second son is named the Great Yakṣa General Jāṅgika;
he commands a host of sixty koṭis of yakṣas and bhūta spirits.
His third son is named the Great Yakṣa General Mahāmaha.
He leads sixty koṭis of yakṣas and bhūta spirits together with his retinue.
His fourth son is named Kumbhodara, the Great Yakṣa General;
he leads sixty koṭis of yakṣas and bhūta spirits together with his retinue.
Maheśvara is a deity with four arms who possesses great majesty and power;
he likewise presides over a host of sixty koṭis of yakṣas, bhūtas, and other spirits.
In this way, the eldest son of Kuvēra, Sanjaya the Great Yakṣa General,
and others, as well as the hosts of Maheśvara and the Gandharvas,
were all completely subdued by means of this divine mantra.
I shall also cause all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and spirits from the ten directions to be subdued;
having bound their bodies with five nooses,
I shall drag them here and destroy them.

The Buddha said: "If there should be another person who receives and maintains this divine mantra according to the Dharma, they should contemplate this Great Radiant Mantra (Mahāvidyārāja) and recite it with a focused mind. Such a divine mantra is able to encompass all other great divine mantras; it is no different from them."
Uttering a wrathful sound and generating a courageous resolve, one should recite this divine mantra.
By the power of the majesty of this divine mantra,
that host of yakṣas and bhūta spirits [will be subdued].
All have been whipped by the iron maces of King Vaiśravaṇa;
bound by their own hands, they come to take refuge and repent.
This applies to all the Māra kings, their hosts of māras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and other spirits.
Within the Buddha-dharma, they constantly perform demonic deeds and give rise to various obstacles and difficulties;
yet, by the power of the majestic virtue of this divine mantra,
in a single moment of thought, they all come of their own accord to take refuge and repent.
Those yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhūta spirits dwell either in the great ocean or in various rivers;
they reside in houses or depend upon doorways.
